etymology: From Saxon bacan, to bake. Hebrew 'aphah is the verb, and the participle 'opheh is a baker — Pharaoh's chief baker in Genesis 40, and the trade street in Jerusalem called the bakers' street (Jeremiah 37:21). Baking is the last step by which grain becomes food, and Scripture watches the whole chain.
biblical_def: Baking is the ordinary work by which grain is made edible, and Scripture keeps it firmly in the world of hospitality, judgment, and folly. Abraham's welcome to three strangers begins in the kitchen: “Make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes upon the hearth” (Genesis 18:6) — an extravagant quantity, prepared in haste, for guests he did not yet know were angels. Israel's hurried departure is preserved in the bread itself: “they baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought forth out of Egypt” (Exodus 12:39), because they were thrust out and could not tarry. Scarcity under covenant curse is described by the ovens: “ten women shall bake your bread in one oven, and they shall deliver you your bread again by weight” (Leviticus 26:26) — one fire for ten households, and bread rationed by the scale. And Isaiah exposes the absurdity of idolatry with a carpenter's log: “he burneth part thereof in the fire; with part thereof he eateth flesh; he roasteth roast, and is satisfied: yea, he warmeth himself, and saith, Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire” (Isaiah 44:16) — the same wood that baked his supper is carved into the god he then worships. The oven, in Scripture, is where generosity, haste, want, and folly all become visible.
webster_summary: To heat and dry, especially to cook bread or cakes in an oven or on a hearth. In Scripture, Sarah's cakes baked in haste for the three strangers, the unleavened cakes baked at the exodus, ten women baking in one oven under judgment, and the wood that both bakes a man's bread and becomes his idol.
webster_full: BAKE, v.t. 1. To heat, dry and harden, as in an oven or furnace, or under coals of fire; to cook by dry heat.
2. To dry and harden by heat, as bricks or earthen vessels.
3. BAKE, v.i. To do the work of baking; as, she brews and bakes.
4. From Saxon bacan, to bake; Hebrew 'aphah, whence 'opheh, a baker.
5. In Scripture, make ready quickly three measures of fine meal, Gen. 18; ten women shall bake your bread in one oven, Lev. 26.
corruption_summary: Hospitality is professionalised into entertainment, so that the plain duty of feeding strangers is left to those with the means to do it impressively; and the folly Isaiah exposes is thought to belong only to ancient idolaters.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is hospitality as a duty rather than a display. Abraham ran to the herd and Sarah worked the dough; Scripture commands the elder to be given to hospitality, tells the church to use hospitality one to another without grudging, and warns that some have entertained angels unawares. What has largely replaced it is entertaining — an occasion arranged when the house is presentable and the table can bear inspection, which by its nature excludes the poor, the awkward, and the unannounced. The New Testament word is philoxenia, love of strangers, and it is aimed precisely at the guest who cannot repay. A loaf baked for someone who arrived without warning discharges the command; a dinner staged for people who will return the invitation does not, and our Lord says as much in Luke 14:12-14.

Isaiah 44 is worth reading whole, because its satire lands closer to home than it appears. A man fells a tree, burns half of it to warm himself and bake his bread, and carves the rest into a god before which he falls down and prays, Deliver me; for thou art my god. Isaiah's comment is not that the man is stupid but that he cannot see it — a deceived heart hath turned him aside. Modern idols are less obviously wooden, which makes the blindness harder to catch: the same money that buys the groceries is trusted for security, the same career that feeds a family is asked to supply significance, and no one notices where the log stopped being fuel and started being a god. The test Isaiah applies is whether the thing can save, and only one Person answers.

etymology: From Saxon grindan, to rub or crush small. The daily grinding of grain between two millstones was women's work, done at dawn, and so constant a sound in a town that Scripture uses its silence as a picture of desolation — the sound of the millstones heard no more.
biblical_def: Grinding is the humblest daily labour in Scripture, and it becomes the measure of three very different things. It is the work of the humiliated: Samson, blinded and shorn, “did grind in the prison house” (Judges 16:21) — a judge of Israel set to a woman's task at a Philistine mill. It is the instrument of a total destruction, when Moses came down from the mount: he took the calf, “and burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it” (Exodus 32:20) — the idol reduced to dust and made to pass through the worshippers. It is the setting of the Lord's warning about the suddenness of His coming: “Two women shall be grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left” (Matthew 24:41) — two women at the same stone, doing the same work, separated for ever in a moment. And it is the prophet's word for what rulers do to the helpless: “What mean ye that ye beat my people to pieces, and grind the faces of the poor? saith the Lord GOD of hosts” (Isaiah 3:15). The mill therefore grinds grain, idols, and men — and God notices which.
webster_summary: To reduce to powder by friction, as grain between millstones; to oppress. In Scripture, Samson grinding in the prison house, the golden calf ground to powder, two women grinding at the mill when the Son of man comes, and rulers who grind the faces of the poor.
webster_full: GRIND, v.t. 1. To break and reduce to fine particles or powder by friction; as, to grind corn between stones.
2. To sharpen by rubbing on a stone; as, to grind an axe.
3. To oppress by severe exactions; to harass; as, to grind the faces of the poor.
4. From Saxon grindan, to grind, to crush small.
5. In Scripture, he did grind in the prison house, Judg. 16; two women shall be grinding at the mill, Matt. 24.
corruption_summary: Oppression is redefined as an impersonal structural force with no guilty parties, so that the prophets' naming of specific rulers who grind the poor is replaced by a category that convicts nobody.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 3:15 is a summons, not a sociological observation. God asks the princes and elders of His people a direct question — what mean ye? — and He names the offence: they have eaten up the vineyard, the spoil of the poor is in their houses, and they grind the faces of the poor. Modern discourse handles oppression very differently. It is treated as a structure, an inherited system, or a set of impersonal forces, so that the wrong is universally deplored and nobody in particular is answerable for it. Scripture's method is the opposite: it names Ahab over Naboth's vineyard, David over Uriah, the merchants who make the ephah small and the shekel great. This matters pastorally as well as politically, because a guilt that belongs to a structure cannot be repented of, and a sin that cannot be repented of cannot be forgiven. The prophets left men with somewhere to go.

The opposite failure is to hear those texts as though the Bible had no such concern at all. It has a great deal — the gleaning laws, the jubilee, the prohibition of usury toward a poor brother, the standing warnings to judges who take a bribe, the sharpness of James against rich men who defraud the labourer of his hire. What Scripture will not do is import an oppressor-oppressed grid as the master key to human society; its categories are sin, the fallen heart, and covenant faithfulness, and it convicts poor and rich alike. The principle to recover is exactly Isaiah's: name real wrongs, name the men who do them, require restitution, and preach to both the rich oppressor and the ground-down poor the same gospel of a Redeemer who is no respecter of persons.

etymology: From Saxon heawan, to cut with blows. Hebrew chatsab is to cut or quarry, used of hewing stone and of digging cisterns out of rock; pasal is to hew or carve, and gives pesel, a graven image — so that the same verb produces the tables of the law and the idols forbidden by them.
biblical_def: Hewing is cutting hard material into a shape a man intends, and Scripture uses it for the noblest and the most futile of human works. God commands it for the second tables: “Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first, and come up unto me into the mount” (Deuteronomy 10:1) — Moses supplies the stone, God supplies the writing, which is the exact division of labour in all true religion. Isaiah uses it to send a discouraged remnant back to their origins: “look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged” (Isaiah 51:1) — remember Abraham, called alone and blessed and increased. Jeremiah uses it for the whole tragedy of the fall: God's people “have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13) — enormous labour in rock, expended to store what a spring gives freely, and the finished work leaks. And it appears at the end of the Gospels in a rich man's generosity: Joseph laid the body “in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock” (Matthew 27:60) — a grave cut at great cost for himself and given away, which its occupant did not need for long.
webster_summary: To cut with an axe or chisel; to shape or quarry hard material by cutting. In Scripture, the two tables of stone Moses was told to hew, the rock whence God's people were hewn, the broken cisterns men hew out for themselves, and the new tomb hewn in the rock.
webster_full: HEW, v.t. 1. To cut with an axe; to fell; as, to hew timber.
2. To chop; to cut in pieces; as, to hew in pieces before the Lord.
3. To form or shape with an edged instrument; to dress, as stone; to quarry.
4. From Saxon heawan, to cut, to strike; Hebrew chatsab, to hew or quarry.
5. In Scripture, hew thee two tables of stone, Deut. 10; hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, Jer. 2.
corruption_summary: Men labour immensely at religion of their own hewing, and the labour itself is taken as proof of sincerity, when Jeremiah's charge is that the finished cistern will not hold water however hard it was cut.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 2:13 names two evils and insists they are two: they have forsaken the fountain of living waters, and they have hewed them out cisterns. The second is not merely the absence of the first; it is a positive and exhausting undertaking. Cutting a cistern out of limestone is heavy work, and men do it because they want water they control — stored, owned, available on their terms — rather than water that must be received from a spring they did not make. That is a fair description of every religion of human construction, from the moralism that trusts its own record to the spirituality assembled privately out of preferences. The labour is real and often sincere. The verdict is that the cistern is broken, and a broken cistern is worse than none, because a man rests on it until the day he is thirsty.

The positive side of the word is worth keeping in view. God told Moses to hew the tables; He did the writing. He tells His people to look to the rock from which they were hewn, that is, to remember that they exist by a call and a promise and not by their own quarrying. And the last hewn thing in the Gospel narrative is a tomb, cut by a rich man for himself, lent to Christ, and vacated on the third day. The principle to recover is the division of labour that runs through the whole of Scripture: men cut, carry, build, and prepare — and what makes any of it holy is that God writes on it. Where that order is reversed, the work may be magnificent and it will still hold no water.

etymology: From Old French diguer, to make a dike or trench. Hebrew chaphar is to dig or search out — the same verb is used of the spies searching the land — and karah is to dig or hollow. Digging in Scripture is patient work in the dark for something not yet visible.
biblical_def: Digging is the labour of a man who believes something is there before he can see it, and Scripture assigns it to the patient and denies it to the slothful. Isaac's work is quiet fidelity to a father's legacy: “Isaac digged again the wells of water, which they had digged in the days of Abraham his father; for the Philistines had stopped them after the death of Abraham” (Genesis 26:18) — not new wells and no new revelation, simply the old springs reopened, which is what reformation always is. Our Lord makes digging the difference between two houses that look identical until the storm: the wise builder “digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock” (Luke 6:48), and the depth was invisible on the day it was dug. The vinedresser pleads for time and offers labour: “let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it” (Luke 13:8) — patient cultivation interceding against the axe. And the unprofitable servant digs for the opposite reason: he “digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money” (Matthew 25:18) — the only man in the parable who used a spade, and he used it to bury a talent rather than to find one.
webster_summary: To open and break or turn up the earth with a spade or mattock; to excavate. In Scripture, Isaac digging again his father's wells, the wise builder who digged deep and laid the foundation on a rock, the vinedresser who would dig about the barren tree, and the servant who digged to hide his lord's money.
webster_full: DIG, v.t. 1. To open, divide or break the earth with a spade, mattock, or other instrument.
2. To excavate; to form by digging; as, to dig a well or a pit.
3. To pierce or open with a snout or by other means, as swine or moles.
4. From Old French diguer, to make a dike; Hebrew chaphar, to dig or search out.
5. In Scripture, Isaac digged again the wells of water, Gen. 26; digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock, Luke 6.
corruption_summary: Depth is treated as optional because it is invisible, so that churches are built to be judged by what shows; and reformation is expected to produce something new rather than to reopen what was stopped up.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 6:48 turns on a detail nobody could photograph. Two houses stand side by side, and until the flood comes there is nothing to distinguish them except what one man did below ground. The parable is the Lord's own commentary on hearing His sayings and doing them, and it is a warning against every form of Christianity built to be inspected. Where a ministry is measured by what can be counted — attendance, buildings, platform — the incentives all run against digging, because digging is expensive, slow, and produces nothing visible. Yet the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock. What is under a man is what will be discovered about him, and the discovery is usually made in a storm.

Isaac's wells correct a different instinct. Faced with springs his father had dug and enemies had stopped with earth, he did not go looking for new water; he cleared out the old wells and called them by the names his father had given them. Every genuine reformation in the church has had that shape. Luther did not invent justification by faith, and the Puritans did not invent the regulative principle; they dug out what had been filled in. The appetite for novelty in doctrine assumes the springs are dry, when what has usually happened is that they have been stopped up by neglect, tradition, or fear. The principle to recover is unglamorous and exact: dig deep, dig old, and expect no one to admire the work until the flood.

etymology: From Hebrew saq through Greek sakkos and Latin saccus — one of the very few words that passed almost unchanged from Hebrew into English. The same word gives us sackcloth, since the coarse haircloth of mourning was the material sacks were made of.
biblical_def: The sack is the plain grain bag of the ancient world, and Scripture makes it the hinge of one of its greatest narratives. Joseph, unrecognised by his brothers, commands a secret restitution: “Then Joseph commanded to fill their sacks with corn, and to restore every man's money into his sack, and to give them provision for the way” (Genesis 42:25) — grain paid for and the payment returned, which terrifies them, because unearned kindness from a man they cannot read is more alarming than a bill. Their reaction is exact: “when both they and their father saw the bundles of money, they were afraid” (Genesis 42:35). The second test is sharper still: “put my cup, the silver cup, in the sack's mouth of the youngest” (Genesis 44:2) — a planted cup designed to discover whether these men would abandon a favoured younger brother as they once abandoned him. And the Gibeonites use sacks to counterfeit a long journey: they “took old sacks upon their asses, and wine bottles, old, and rent, and bound up” (Joshua 9:4) — a deception that worked because Joshua asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. Sacks in Scripture carry grain, hidden mercy, planted evidence, and outright fraud — and in each case what is in the sack is not what it appears.
webster_summary: A bag, usually of coarse cloth, for holding grain or goods. In Scripture, the sacks Joseph filled with corn and secretly with his brothers' money, the sack in which the silver cup was planted, and the old sacks by which the Gibeonites feigned a long journey.
webster_full: SACK, n. 1. A bag, usually of coarse cloth, for holding and conveying corn, wool, and other commodities.
2. The quantity contained in a sack; a definite measure of certain goods.
3. Sackcloth; coarse cloth worn in mourning and humiliation.
4. From Hebrew saq, a sack or sackcloth; Greek sakkos; Latin saccus.
5. In Scripture, fill their sacks with corn, Gen. 42; put my cup in the sack's mouth of the youngest, Gen. 44.
corruption_summary: Joseph's dealings with his brothers are read as vengeance dressed up as testing, missing that every hard thing he did was aimed at producing repentance rather than punishment.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the difference between testing and revenge. Joseph had absolute power, a legitimate grievance, and every opportunity; what he did with it was to return their money, feed their households, seat Benjamin in honour, and construct one final test to discover whether the men who sold a favoured brother would now surrender another. When Judah offered himself as a bondman in Benjamin's place, the test was complete and Joseph could not refrain himself. His own summary removes any doubt about his motive: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good. The severity was real, it was temporary, and it was aimed at their repentance — which is exactly how God deals with His own people, and why the hardest providences in a believer's life are so often followed by a revelation of the hand behind them.

The Gibeonites' sacks preach a plainer lesson. Their fraud was elaborate — mouldy bread, patched shoes, cracked wineskins, worn-out sacks — and it succeeded for one stated reason: the men of Israel took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. The evidence was inspected and the LORD was not consulted, and Israel was bound by an oath she had been deceived into swearing and afterwards kept. The lesson is not that appearances always lie but that appearances are not enough, and that a decision made on inspection alone will eventually meet the facts. Joshua's honouring of the oath, once made, is the second half of the account and no less instructive.

etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps British. Hebrew has several: sal, the woven basket of the consecration offerings; tene', the basket of firstfruits carried to the sanctuary; kelub, a cage or fruit basket. Greek distinguishes kophinos, the small hand basket a Jew carried on a journey, from spuris, a large hamper big enough to hold a man.
biblical_def: Baskets in Scripture carry what is given to God, what God gives back, and occasionally a man. The firstfruits went up in one: “thou shalt take of the first of all the fruit of the earth... and shalt put it in a basket, and shalt go unto the place which the LORD thy God shall choose” (Deuteronomy 26:2) — the confession of faith that follows it is one of the oldest in the Bible. The consecration of Aaron used another: “thou shalt put them into one basket, and bring them in the basket” (Exodus 29:3). After the feeding of the five thousand the arithmetic is deliberately preserved: “they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full” (Matthew 14:20) — twelve kophinoi, one apparently for each disciple who had said it could not be done. Amos is shown one as a pun on the end of a nation: “behold a basket of summer fruit” (Amos 8:1), ripe and about to spoil. And Paul's first exploit as a Christian is an undignified escape: “then the disciples took him by night, and let him down by the wall in a basket” (Acts 9:25) — the great apostle's ministry begins with him being lowered out of a city in a hamper, a detail he later cites as something to glory in.
webster_summary: A vessel made of twigs, rushes, or splints interwoven. In Scripture, the basket of firstfruits carried to the sanctuary, the basket of the consecration offerings, the twelve baskets of fragments after the feeding of the five thousand, the basket of summer fruit shown to Amos, and the basket in which Paul was let down the wall.
webster_full: BASKET, n. 1. A domestic vessel made of twigs, rushes, splinters or other flexible things interwoven.
2. The contents of a basket; as much as a basket will contain.
3. In Scripture, baskets were used for carrying fruit, bread, and the offerings of the sanctuary.
4. Of uncertain origin; perhaps of British derivation.
5. In Scripture, put it in a basket, Deut. 26; they took up twelve baskets full, Matt. 14.
corruption_summary: The twelve baskets are treated as a pleasant detail rather than as evidence, and the miracle itself is explained away as a lesson in sharing; while firstfruits giving is reduced to a technique for obtaining return.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard liberal handling of the feeding of the five thousand is that the real miracle was generosity: a boy shared his lunch, the crowd was shamed into producing hidden provisions, and everyone ate. The account resists it at every point. The disciples state the problem in monetary terms — two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient — and the surplus is the difficulty for the theory, because leftovers do not accumulate when people eat what they brought. Twelve baskets full of fragments after five thousand men, beside women and children, is the evangelists' way of establishing that something was created and not merely distributed. John records the crowd's own conclusion, that this is of a truth that prophet that should come into the world, and their attempt to take Him by force and make Him king — not the reaction of people who had shared sandwiches.

The basket of firstfruits carries a different corruption. Deuteronomy 26 has the worshipper bring the first of the harvest, set it before the altar, and recite what God has done: a Syrian ready to perish was my father, and the LORD brought us out. The giving is a confession, and it is first — before the rest is counted, and therefore before the giver knows whether the year will be good. Prosperity teaching inverts this, presenting the first gift as seed sown for a guaranteed return and turning worship into investment. The principle to recover is the order of the passage: God acted, the worshipper remembers, the basket follows, and the giving is thanksgiving for a redemption already accomplished rather than a deposit against a harvest not yet in.
roots_summary: Hebrew sal, a woven basket for bread and offerings; tene', the firstfruits basket; kelub, a fruit basket or cage; Greek kophinos, a hand basket, and spuris, a large hamper.

Of the surplus that proves the miracle: they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full (Matthew 14:20).

etymology: From French bouteille, Late Latin butticula, a small cask. In Scripture a bottle is almost never glass: it is a skin, usually a goatskin, sewn and sealed and used for water, milk, or wine — which is why an old one cracks, and why a new wine still working will burst it.
biblical_def: The bottle of Scripture is a skin, and every biblical use depends on that. Hagar is sent away with one: “Abraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread, and a bottle of water, and gave it unto Hagar” (Genesis 21:14) — a skin of water in a wilderness, and God met her when it was spent. Elihu describes the pressure of unspoken words in the same terms: “my belly is as wine which hath no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles” (Job 32:19). The Psalmist smoke-dries into uselessness: “I am become like a bottle in the smoke; yet do I not forget thy statutes” (Psalm 119:83) — a skin left hanging in the rafters, shrivelled and cracked, and still holding to the word. And the Lord Jesus takes the everyday fact of fermentation to explain why His gospel could not be poured into the forms of Pharisaic religion: “neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved” (Matthew 9:17). Most tender of all is David's: “put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?” (Psalm 56:8) — God keeping a man's weeping as carefully as a man keeps wine.
webster_summary: A vessel for holding liquids, in Scripture usually made of skin. In Scripture, the bottle of water given to Hagar, the bottle in the smoke to which the afflicted Psalmist likens himself, the new wine that bursts old bottles, and the bottle in which God is asked to put a man's tears.
webster_full: BOTTLE, n. 1. A hollow vessel of glass, wood, leather or other material, with a narrow mouth, for holding liquors.
2. The contents of a bottle; as much as a bottle contains.
3. In Scripture, a vessel made of the skin of a goat or kid, sewed and pitched.
4. From French bouteille, Late Latin butticula, a small cask.
5. In Scripture, a bottle of water, Gen. 21; new wine into old bottles, Matt. 9; put thou my tears into thy bottle, Ps. 56.
corruption_summary: The new-wine saying is enlisted to justify whatever a generation wishes to discard, as though novelty were the point; when the new wine is the gospel of Christ and the old bottles are the forms of a religion of works.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 9:17 is quoted constantly to sanctify change — new music, new structures, new doctrine — on the assumption that the old bottles are whatever the previous generation valued. That is not what the passage is about. The question put to Christ concerned fasting: why do John's disciples and the Pharisees fast, but thy disciples fast not? His answer is that the bridegroom is present, and that the new covenant He is bringing cannot be poured into the forms of a system built on ceremonial observance and human merit. The new wine is the gospel; the old bottles are the Pharisaic religion of works, and the point is that the two cannot be combined without destroying both. Nothing in the saying makes novelty a virtue or age a fault. Paul told the churches to hold the traditions they had been taught, and Jeremiah told a wandering people to ask for the old paths, where is the good way.

Read rightly, the saying is a warning against exactly the syncretism the modern church attempts most often — grafting the gospel onto a system it cannot inhabit. Where evangelical language is poured into a therapeutic framework, or a sacramental system of merit, or a political programme, the container shapes what it holds until the wine is unrecognisable. The bottles break and the wine runs out, which is why doctrinal drift so often ends in a denomination that retains its buildings and its vocabulary and has lost the thing itself. The principle to recover is that the gospel supplies its own forms: preaching, the ordinances, discipline, prayer, the fellowship of the saints — new bottles for new wine, and both are preserved.
roots_summary: Hebrew chemeth, a waterskin; nod, a skin bottle for milk or wine; nebel, an earthen jar or skin; Greek askos, a leathern wine skin.
roots_lines: Hebrew chemeth (H2573) — a skin bottle for water; the one Abraham gave Hagar (Genesis 21:14).
Hebrew nod (H4997) — a skin bottle; “put thou my tears into thy bottle” (Psalm 56:8).
Hebrew nebel (H5035) — a jar or skin for wine; also the name of a stringed instrument shaped like it.
Hebrew 'ob (H178) — a bottle or skin, and by a dark extension the word for a familiar spirit, as of a hollow murmuring vessel.
Greek askos (G779) — a leathern bottle or wineskin; the old and new bottles of Matthew 9:17.
usage: Of provision that runs out and a God who does not: took bread, and a bottle of water, and gave it unto Hagar (Genesis 21:14).
Of affliction that has not let go of the word: I am become like a bottle in the smoke; yet do I not forget thy statutes (Psalm 119:83).
Of the gospel and the forms it cannot inhabit: neither do men put new wine into old bottles (Matthew 9:17).

Behold, my belly is as wine which hath no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles.

etymology: Of northern origin, Saxon baelg, a bag or skin — the same root as belly and bellows. In Scripture the bag is chiefly the merchant's purse in which weights were carried, and thereby becomes the standing symbol of honesty or fraud in trade.
biblical_def: Because a merchant carried his weights in a bag, Scripture makes the bag the test of commercial honesty. The standard is stated as God's own: “A just weight and balance are the LORD's: all the weights of the bag are his work” (Proverbs 16:11) — not a civic convention but a divine ordinance, so that a rigged scale is blasphemy in miniature. Micah puts the question to a nation as a prosecutor: “Shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights?” (Micah 6:11). Haggai diagnoses a whole economy that will not prosper because the people build their own houses and leave God's in ruins: “he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes” (Haggai 1:6) — a sentence every generation has recognised. David carried a humbler one to the valley of Elah: he chose five smooth stones “and put them in a shepherd's bag which he had, even in a scrip; and his sling was in his hand” (1 Samuel 17:40). And the darkest bag in Scripture belonged to the treasurer of the apostolic company: Judas “was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein” (John 12:6) — a man trusted with the money of the Son of God, stealing from it, and betraying Him for thirty pieces of silver.
webster_summary: A sack or pouch of cloth or leather for holding goods, money, or weights. In Scripture, the bag whose weights are the LORD's work, the bag of deceitful weights God will not count pure, the bag with holes into which unblessed wages are put, David's shepherd's bag, and the bag Judas carried and stole from.
webster_full: BAG, n. 1. A sack; a pouch, usually of cloth or leather, used to hold, preserve or convey corn, money and other articles.
2. A sort of silken purse formerly tied to men's hair behind.
3. In commerce, a certain quantity of a commodity, as much as a bag will hold.
4. From Saxon baelg, a bag or skin; the same root as belly and bellows.
5. In Scripture, all the weights of the bag are his work, Prov. 16; he was a thief, and had the bag, John 12.
corruption_summary: Commercial fraud is treated as a regulatory matter rather than a sin against God, so that men obey the law of the land in trade and never consider that the weights themselves are the LORD's work.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 16:11 makes a startling claim about a mundane thing: all the weights of the bag are His work. Honest measure is not a civic convention that societies adopt for convenience; it is God's ordinance, and a false weight is therefore an offence against Him before it is an offence against a customer. Scripture returns to this with unusual frequency — divers weights and divers measures are an abomination unto the LORD, the ephah made small and the shekel great, the balances of deceit in the merchant's hand — and the vehemence is instructive. Modern business ethics locates the wrong in harm to the consumer or in breach of regulation, which leaves a man free wherever the harm is untraceable or the regulation silent. The biblical location of the wrong is in God's ownership of the standard, and that convicts in private as well as in public.

Judas supplies the sharpest warning in Scripture about money in religious hands. He kept the bag for the Lord and the twelve; he was trusted, he was not suspected, and he objected to Mary's ointment in the language of concern for the poor while stealing from the fund. John states both facts in one sentence, and the juxtaposition is the point: the man's cover was charity. Every church that handles money is under the same exposure, which is why Paul took pains to have the collection for Jerusalem carried by men chosen by the churches, providing for honest things not only in the sight of the Lord but also in the sight of men. The principle to recover is that transparency is not a modern imposition on ministry; it is apostolic practice, adopted precisely because a bag in the wrong hands has ruined better men than most.
roots_summary: Hebrew kīs, a purse or bag for weights; tserōr, a bundle or pouch; yalqut, a shepherd's scrip; Greek glōssokomon, a money box, and ballantion, a purse.
roots_lines: Hebrew kīs (H3599) — a bag or purse, especially for weights; “all the weights of the bag are his work” (Proverbs 16:11).
Hebrew tserōr (H6872) — a bundle or pouch; “bound in the bundle of life” (1 Samuel 25:29).

Greek glōssokomon (G1101) — a case or money box; the bag Judas carried (John 12:6; 13:29).
Greek ballantion (G905) — a purse; “provide yourselves bags which wax not old” (Luke 12:33).

Of wages that will not stay: he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes (Haggai 1:6).
Of trusted hands that stole: he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein (John 12:6).

A just weight and balance are the LORD'S: all the weights of the bag are his work.
Micah 6:11

etymology: From Saxon cist, Latin cista, Greek kistē, a box or coffer. The Hebrew 'arōn that is rendered chest in the temple-repair narratives is the same word rendered ark elsewhere — the ark of the covenant and Joseph's coffin are both 'arōn, a made box for keeping something.
biblical_def: The chest enters Scripture as a piece of financial reform. Jehoash found the temple in disrepair and the priests' collection system failing, so a simple mechanism was installed: “But Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in the lid of it, and set it beside the altar, on the right side as one cometh into the house of the LORD: and the priests that kept the door put therein all the money that was brought into the house of the LORD” (2 Kings 12:9). The chronicler records the same reform under Joash with the king's command attached: “And at the king's commandment they made a chest, and set it without at the gate of the house of the LORD” (2 Chronicles 24:8) — and the people rejoiced and brought in until the chest was full, repeatedly. The word appears once more in a very different setting, among the luxury goods of Tyre's trade: “these were thy merchants in all sorts of things, in blue clothes, and broidered work, and in chests of rich apparel, bound with cords” (Ezekiel 27:24) — a city whose chests held finery, and whose end the prophet then describes. A chest keeps what is put in it. Whether that is money brought willingly for the house of God, or the wardrobe of a merchant empire about to sink, is the whole of the difference.
webster_summary: A box of wood or other material, usually with a lid, for holding goods or money. In Scripture, the chest Jehoiada bored and set beside the altar for the repair of the house of the LORD, the chest set at the gate at the king's commandment, and the chests of rich apparel among the merchandise of Tyre.
webster_full: CHEST, n. 1. A box of wood or other material, in which goods are kept or transported.
2. A coffer; a strong box for holding money or valuables.
3. The trunk of the body from the neck to the belly; the thorax.
4. From Saxon cist, Latin cista, Greek kiste, a box or coffer.
5. In Scripture, took a chest, and bored a hole in the lid of it, 2 Kings 12; chests of rich apparel, Ezek. 27.
corruption_summary: Giving is either extracted by pressure and appeal, or neglected altogether as unspiritual, when the reform under Joash shows willing gifts, a plain mechanism, and honest accounting working together.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the shape of the reform itself. The old system had failed — the priests had collected for years and the breaches of the house were not repaired — so Jehoiada installed a chest with a hole in the lid where everyone could see it, set it beside the altar, and had the king's scribe and the high priest count the money together and put it up in bags. Then the funds went straight to the workmen: carpenters, builders, masons, hewers of stone. And the narrative adds a striking detail — they reckoned not with the men into whose hand they delivered the money to be bestowed on workmen, for they dealt faithfully. Willing gifts, a visible mechanism, joint counting, and men of proven character: a plainer manual for church finance has never been written.

Both modern failures are corrected by it. Where money is raised by pressure — emotional appeal, guaranteed return, public ranking of givers — the giving is no longer the free thanksgiving Scripture describes, and it corrodes both giver and ministry. Where the subject is avoided entirely as unspiritual, the house of God falls into disrepair while its people prosper, which is precisely the situation Haggai confronted. The chest stood beside the altar in plain view, and the people rejoiced to fill it. Giving that is glad, informed, and honestly handled is not a distraction from worship; in 2 Chronicles 24 it is what a revival looked like.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'arōn, a box, coffer, chest, or ark; genez, a chest or treasury; Greek kistē, a box, the origin of the English word.

etymology: From Old French plate, a flat vessel, from Greek platus, broad or flat. The Greek paropsis was strictly a side dish, the vessel in which delicacies were served beside the main course — a detail that gives the Lord's rebuke its edge, since it was the finest dish in the house that the Pharisees polished most carefully.
biblical_def: The platter appears in Scripture at one moment only, and it is used to expose a whole religion. Our Lord pronounces the woe: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess” (Matthew 23:25). Then He gives the remedy in the same figure: “Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also” (Matthew 23:26) — note the order, and note that the outside is not despised but is said to follow. Luke records the same charge at a Pharisee's own table, where the host had marvelled that Christ did not wash before dinner: “Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness” (Luke 11:39). And Luke preserves the counsel that follows, which is startling: “But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you” (Luke 11:41) — the man whose inside is right will open his hand, and generosity is offered as the test and evidence of a cleansed interior. The dish is a picture of a man: what is served from it is what was inside, however carefully the rim was wiped.
webster_summary: A large shallow dish for holding food; in Greek usage a side dish for delicacies. In Scripture, the cup and platter the Pharisees cleaned on the outside while full of extortion within, and the Lord's command to cleanse first what is inside the platter.
webster_full: PLATTER, n. 1. A large shallow dish or plate for holding meat and other eatables.
2. One who plats or forms by weaving; a maker of plats.
3. In Scripture, the vessel from which food was served at table, contrasted with the heart of the man who served it.
4. From Old French plate, from Greek platus, broad or flat.
5. In Scripture, ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, Matt. 23; cleanse first that which is within, Matt. 23.
corruption_summary: The rebuke is heard as a general dismissal of outward observance, so that carelessness in conduct is defended as inwardness; when Christ's command is to clean the inside so that the outside may be clean also.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 23:26 is more often quoted than finished. The Lord says cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also — a purpose clause the popular use of the verse omits entirely. The common misreading turns the woe into a licence: since God looks on the heart, external conduct, reverence, doctrine, and church order are secondary matters that a sincere man may hold loosely. That is not what was said to the Pharisees, and the same chapter proves it: of their scrupulous tithing of mint and anise and cummin He says these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. The charge was never that they were too careful outwardly. It was that the care stopped at the rim while extortion and excess sat inside, so that the whole apparatus had become a way of not dealing with God.

Luke's version supplies the test, and it is not the one a religious man would choose: give alms of such things as ye have, and behold, all things are clean unto you. This is not the purchase of cleanness by charity — Scripture nowhere allows that — but the exposure of the heart by its grip on possessions. Extortion and ravening are what filled the Pharisees' dishes, and the sign of a cleansed interior is a hand that opens. The principle to recover joins the two halves without compromise: the inside first, always, because that is where God begins and where the man actually is; and then the outside genuinely, because a clean heart does not stay hidden and has never yet produced a careless life.
roots_summary: Greek paropsis, a side dish or the delicacy served in it; pinax, a plank, board, or platter; potērion, the cup paired with it in the woe.

Greek harpagē (G724) — extortion, plunder, ravening; what filled the inside of the Pharisees' vessels.
Greek akrasia (G192) — want of self-control, excess; joined to extortion in Matthew 23:25.
Greek eleēmosynē (G1654) — alms, an act of mercy; the evidence Christ calls for in Luke 11:41.

Of the test of a cleansed heart: give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you (Luke 11:41).
